title: Road construction & maintenance
summary: The three coats are distinguished by what lies BELOW them — prime coat on a granular base, tack coat between bituminous layers, seal coat on the finished surface — and that single question settles most of the construction items. For maintenance, each distress maps to a specific cause, so a question naming a symptom is asking for it: alligator cracking means fatigue, rutting means deformation, bleeding means too much binder, ravelling means too little. In Nepal, hill road drainage is the maintenance activity that matters most, because most failures are water-triggered.

sections.heading: Earthwork and the formation
sections.body:
**The construction sequence** for a new road:

> **Setting out → Clearing and grubbing → Earthwork (cutting and filling) → Subgrade preparation → Sub-base → Base course → Prime coat → Binder course → Tack coat → Wearing course → Seal coat → Shoulders, drainage and furniture**

**Earthwork** is the largest single item on a hill road and the source of most of its environmental damage.

| Operation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clearing and grubbing** | Removal of vegetation, topsoil and roots; topsoil **stockpiled for reuse** on slopes |
| **Cutting** | Excavation to formation level; side slopes by soil and rock type |
| **Filling (embankment)** | In **compacted layers of 200–300 mm**, each tested |
| **Blasting** | In rock; **controlled blasting** near structures and slopes |
| **Spoil disposal** | To **designed tips**, not down the slope |

**Side slopes:**

| Material | Cutting | Filling |
|---|---|---|
| Hard rock | **1/4:1 to vertical** | — |
| Soft rock | 1/2:1 | — |
| **Ordinary soil** | **1:1 to 1.5:1** | **1.5:1 to 2:1** |
| Loose or sandy soil | 2:1 | 2:1 to 3:1 |

**Filling always takes flatter slopes than cutting** in the same material, because a fill is remoulded, less consolidated, and must be stable under its own weight and any seepage through it.

**Benching** is used where a cut or fill is high: horizontal berms **3–5 m wide at 5–8 m vertical intervals** break the slope, **intercept surface water**, catch falling material, and provide access for maintenance. A single continuous high slope both erodes faster and fails more catastrophically.

**Spoil disposal deserves the emphasis it rarely receives.** Tipping excavated material down the hillside — the cheapest and commonest practice — causes damage far exceeding the road's own footprint:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Buries fields, forest and terraces** below | Direct loss of productive land |
| **Blocks streams and drainage lines** | Ponding, then a debris flow when the blockage fails |
| **Loads the slope below with unstable debris** | Fails in the next monsoon, often taking the slope with it |
| **Increases the sediment load** of the river | Aggradation downstream, raising flood levels |

**The correct practice** — **designated spoil tips at identified stable locations, with a retaining structure at the toe, drainage, and revegetation** — costs money and is routinely omitted. It is a clear case where the engineering obligation and the environmental one coincide exactly.

**Compaction of the embankment and subgrade:**

| Layer | Compaction requirement |
|---|---|
| **Embankment body** | ≥ **95%** of modified Proctor MDD |
| **Subgrade (top 500 mm)** | ≥ **97%**, or **100%** on a major road |
| Sub-base and base | 98 – 100% |

**Compaction is done at or near the OMC** — too dry and the target density cannot be reached at any effort, too wet and the soil **shears and pumps** under the roller rather than densifying.

**Matching the roller to the material** is the practical skill, and the pairing is examinable:

| Roller | Mechanism | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Smooth wheeled (static)** | Direct pressure | **Granular** soils, finishing, WBM |
| **Pneumatic tyred** | **Kneading** action | Wide range, including **bituminous** layers |
| **Sheep foot (pad foot)** | **Kneading** with high contact pressure | **COHESIVE** soils — clay |
| **Vibratory** | **Rearranges** particles by vibration | **GRANULAR** soils — sand, gravel, rock fill |
| Impact / rammer, plate compactor | Confined areas | Trenches, around structures |

**Sheep foot for clay and vibratory for granular** is the pairing to hold, and the reason is the mechanism: **cohesive** soils need to be **kneaded** so the clay lumps are broken down and remoulded, which the pad feet do; **granular** soils need their particles **shaken into a denser packing**, which vibration does and static pressure does not. A vibratory roller on wet clay simply bounces; a sheep foot on sand walks out of it.

**Field density control** by **core cutter** (soft fine-grained soil) or **sand replacement** (gravelly or hard soil, where the core cutter cannot be driven), computing **relative compaction = field dry density ÷ laboratory maximum dry density**.

sections.heading: Pavement construction
sections.body:
**Granular layers:**

| Layer | Method |
|---|---|
| **GSB (granular sub-base)** | Graded material spread and compacted; provides **drainage** as well as strength |
| **WBM (Water Bound Macadam)** | Coarse aggregate spread, **screenings** filled in, **water** applied, and rolled; laid in layers of **75 mm compacted thickness** |
| **WMM (Wet Mix Macadam)** | Graded aggregate **premixed with water in a plant**, spread by paver, compacted |

**WMM has largely replaced WBM** on major work, and the reasons are direct: **plant mixing gives a uniform gradation and moisture content**, the paver gives better level control, and construction is much faster. WBM's screenings-and-water process is labour-intensive and its quality depends on the care taken in filling the voids — which in practice varies. WBM survives on low-volume and rural roads where plant is unavailable and labour is cheap.

**The three bituminous coats** — the most examined item in the subchapter, and the distinguishing question is simply **what lies BELOW**:

| Coat | Applied ON | Purpose | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PRIME coat** | A **GRANULAR (non-bituminous) base** | **PENETRATES and seals** the surface voids; binds the loose fines; provides a **bond** for the layer above | **7 – 10 kg/10 m²** |
| **TACK coat** | An **existing BITUMINOUS surface**, or a primed surface | **BONDS two bituminous layers** together | **2 – 3 kg/10 m²** |
| **SEAL coat** | The **FINISHED surface** | **WATERPROOFS** and provides **texture** | Varies with type |

**So the sequence through the pavement is:**

> subgrade → sub-base → base course → **PRIME COAT** → binder course → **TACK COAT** → wearing course → **SEAL COAT**

**Why a prime coat is needed at all.** A granular base is **porous and dusty**. Without priming: the bituminous layer above **does not bond** and can slip or delaminate; **water enters** the base through the voids; and **dust on the surface prevents adhesion entirely**.

**Why a tack coat cannot substitute for it.** A tack coat is **more viscous** and designed to remain **on** the surface as a sticky film — it does not penetrate. On a porous granular base it would sit on top of the dust and fail to seal the voids. Each coat is formulated for its own job, and using the wrong one produces a pavement that delaminates.

**Practical requirements:** the surface must be **clean, dry and swept** before priming; the primed surface is left to **CURE until it is tacky but not runny** before the next layer; and traffic is kept off. Laying a bituminous layer onto an **uncured or dusty prime coat** is a common cause of early **delamination**.

**Bituminous surfacings, from thin to thick:**

| Surfacing | Thickness | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface dressing** | A sprayed binder plus chippings | **Waterproofing and skid resistance only — NOT structural** |
| **Premix carpet** | 20 mm | Thin wearing course, usually with a seal coat |
| **Mix seal surfacing** | 20 mm | Better graded than premix carpet |
| **BM (bituminous macadam)** | 50 – 75 mm | Open graded base or binder course |
| **DBM (dense bituminous macadam)** | 50 – 100 mm | **Dense graded binder course — structural** |
| **SDBC / BC (bituminous concrete)** | 25 – 50 mm | **Dense graded wearing course — the highest quality** |

**Surface dressing being non-structural is the point most often missed.** It seals the surface and restores skid resistance, but it **adds no strength**. A structurally inadequate pavement is therefore **not improved** by surface dressing — only protected from water while it continues to deteriorate. Applying surface dressing to a cracked, deforming pavement is a common and futile expenditure.

**Laying and compacting a bituminous layer** — the temperatures matter and are examinable:

| Stage | Temperature |
|---|---|
| **Mixing** | **150 – 165 °C** |
| **Laying** | **≥ 130 °C** |
| **Rolling — start** | **≥ 100 – 110 °C** |
| **Rolling — complete before** | **≈ 80 °C** |

**Compaction must be completed while the mix is hot**, because a cooled bituminous mix is too stiff to be densified — and an under-compacted layer has **high air voids**, which lets water and air in, **oxidises and hardens the binder**, and leads to early **ravelling and cracking**. Laying in cold or wet weather, or hauling too far, causes exactly this.

**Rolling sequence**: **breakdown rolling** (steel wheeled, immediately behind the paver), **intermediate rolling** (pneumatic tyred, the main densification), **finish rolling** (steel wheeled, to remove marks). Rolling proceeds from the **lower edge toward the higher** on a superelevated section, with each pass overlapping the last.

**Joints** in bituminous work — longitudinal and transverse — are the weak points: they must be **cut back to a vertical face, cleaned, painted with a tack coat and properly compacted**, or they open and admit water. Most bituminous surfaces fail first at a joint.

**Quality control** during construction:

| Item | Test |
|---|---|
| Aggregate | Grading, shape, strength, water absorption |
| Binder | Penetration or viscosity, softening point |
| **Mix** | **Binder content (extraction test)**, gradation after extraction, **Marshall stability and flow** |
| **Laid layer** | **Thickness**, **density (core cutting)**, **air voids**, surface **level and regularity** |
| Surface | **Roughness (bump integrator, roughometer)**, texture depth, skid resistance |

**Core cutting from the finished layer** is the definitive check on both **thickness** and **compaction**, and it is the test contractors most dislike — which is a reason to insist on it.

sections.heading: Pavement distresses and their causes
sections.body:
**Each distress maps to a specific cause**, so a question naming the symptom is asking for the cause. This table is the most valuable content in the subchapter.

**Flexible pavement distresses:**

| Distress | Appearance | **Cause** |
|---|---|---|
| **Alligator (fatigue) cracking** | Interconnected cracks in a crocodile-skin pattern, in the **wheel paths** | **FATIGUE from repeated loading** — the pavement is structurally inadequate for the traffic it has carried |
| **Longitudinal cracking** | Cracks parallel to the centre line | Poor **joint** construction, differential settlement, or the start of fatigue |
| **Transverse cracking** | Across the carriageway | **Thermal** contraction, binder hardening, or **reflection** from a joint below |
| **Reflection cracking** | Mirroring the joints of an underlying rigid layer | Movement at the joint below |
| **Edge cracking** | Along the pavement edge | **Inadequate shoulder support**, poor edge drainage |
| **RUTTING** | Longitudinal depressions in the **wheel paths** | **Permanent deformation** — of the subgrade (inadequate thickness), or of the mix (**excess binder**, soft binder, poor aggregate) |
| **Shoving / corrugation** | Ripples or bulges, at braking and turning locations | **Unstable mix** — excess binder, rounded aggregate, poor bond to the layer below |
| **BLEEDING (flushing)** | A shiny black film of binder on the surface | **TOO MUCH BINDER**, or too soft a grade for the temperature |
| **RAVELLING** | Progressive loss of aggregate from the surface | **TOO LITTLE BINDER**, poor compaction, **stripping**, or aged and brittle binder |
| **POTHOLE** | A bowl-shaped hole | **Water entering** through a crack, weakening the layers, then traffic removing the material |
| **Depression / settlement** | A local low area | Subgrade settlement, poor compaction, a buried utility trench |
| **Stripping** | The binder separates from the aggregate | **WATER** plus a hydrophilic (siliceous) aggregate, or a damp aggregate at mixing |
| **Polishing** | A smooth, slippery surface | Aggregate with a low **polished stone value** |

**The rutting–bleeding–ravelling trio is the one to hold**, because all three relate to the binder content and they point in different directions:

> **RUTTING and BLEEDING → TOO MUCH binder (or too soft).**
> **RAVELLING and CRACKING → TOO LITTLE binder (or too hard, or aged).**

That is precisely the balance the **Marshall design at 4% air voids** exists to strike, and it is why the optimum binder content is neither a maximum nor a minimum.

**And the two crack types:**

> **ALLIGATOR cracking is a STRUCTURAL failure** — the pavement is too thin for its traffic, and an overlay is needed.
> **TRANSVERSE and BLOCK cracking are usually a MATERIAL failure** — thermal or ageing — and a surface treatment may suffice.

Distinguishing them decides whether the remedy is a **structural overlay** or a **surface treatment**, which is a large difference in cost.

**Rigid pavement distresses:**

| Distress | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Cracking** — transverse, longitudinal, corner | Overloading, inadequate thickness, **warping stress**, poor joint spacing |
| **Faulting** (a step at a joint) | **Loss of load transfer** across the joint; pumping |
| **PUMPING** | Water beneath the slab is **ejected through the joint** under load, carrying fines with it — progressively **removing the support** |
| **Spalling** at joints | Poor joint construction; incompressible material in the joint |
| **Blow-up** | Expansion with no room to move; incompressibles in the expansion joint |
| Scaling, polishing | Poor concrete quality; inadequate curing |
| Joint seal failure | Age; leads to water and grit entry |

**Pumping is the characteristic rigid pavement failure**, and its mechanism is self-accelerating: water beneath the slab is **ejected under load through the joint**, carrying **subgrade fines** with it; the loss of fines creates a **void under the slab edge**; the slab then deflects more, pumping harder; and eventually the unsupported corner **cracks**. Prevention is by a **non-erodible sub-base (DLC)**, good **drainage**, and **effective joint sealing** to keep the water out.

**Maintenance categories:**

| Category | Character |
|---|---|
| **Routine** | Continuous minor work — **drain clearance**, pothole patching, crack sealing, vegetation control, sign and marking upkeep |
| **Periodic** | At intervals of a few years — **renewal of the surfacing**, surface dressing, seal coat |
| **Special / emergency** | **Landslide clearance**, flood damage, accident damage |
| **Rehabilitation / strengthening** | **Structural overlay**, reconstruction |

**Maintenance treatments:**

| Treatment | For |
|---|---|
| **Crack sealing** | Cracks below about 3 mm — keeps water out; **the highest-return maintenance there is** |
| **Pothole patching** | Cut to a **regular shape with vertical sides**, remove all loose material, tack coat, fill and compact in layers |
| **Surface dressing / renewal** | Restoring waterproofing and skid resistance |
| **Overlay** | Structural strengthening, designed by Benkelman beam or FWD |
| **Milling and inlay** | Removing a deformed layer and replacing it |
| **Recycling** | Reusing the existing material, hot or cold, in place or in a plant |

**Crack sealing gives the highest return of any maintenance activity**, and the reason is the whole logic of pavement maintenance: **water is what destroys a pavement**. A 2 mm crack sealed for a few rupees per metre prevents the water ingress that would otherwise soften the layers, strip the binder, and become a pothole costing a hundred times as much — and then a failed section costing a thousand times as much.

> **The economics of maintenance are steeply non-linear: work deferred does not merely wait, it multiplies.**

That is the argument for **preventive maintenance**, and it is why a road authority that spends its budget on emergency repairs is always short of money — it is paying the multiplied price of work not done earlier.

**Pavement condition assessment:**

| Measure | Method |
|---|---|
| **Roughness** | **Bump integrator, roughometer, or laser profiler**; expressed as the **IRI (International Roughness Index)** |
| **Structural capacity** | **Benkelman beam** or **FWD** deflection |
| **Distress survey** | Visual, mapped by type, severity and extent |
| **Skid resistance** | Portable skid tester, SCRIM |
| Rut depth | Straight edge or profiler |

**Roughness matters more than it appears**, because it is what the **road user actually experiences and pays for**: vehicle operating costs, travel time and comfort all depend on it far more than on the pavement's structural condition. A **Pavement Management System** uses roughness and distress data to prioritise work across a network, allocating a limited budget where it yields the greatest reduction in total transport cost.

sections.heading: Hill road construction, drainage and maintenance
sections.body:
**Hill road construction methods:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Full bench cut** | The **whole formation cut into the hillside**; **no fill** — the most stable, but the greatest excavation and spoil |
| **Part cut, part fill (half bench)** | Formation partly in cut, partly on fill; **less excavation** but the **fill portion is the weak part** |
| Full fill | Rare; unstable on a steep slope |
| **Retaining structures** | Gabion, masonry or RCC walls to support the fill or the cut |

**Full bench cut is more stable but generates more spoil**; part cut and fill balances the earthwork but the **fill side is where hill roads subside**, because fill on a steep slope is difficult to compact and is undermined by drainage. The choice therefore depends on the slope angle, the material, and — critically — on whether the spoil can be disposed of responsibly.

**The green road concept**, developed in Nepal, deserves mention as a genuine local contribution: hill roads built with **labour-intensive methods, minimal blasting, balanced cut and fill, bio-engineering and construction spread over several seasons** — allowing the slopes to stabilise between phases. It is slower and produces a narrower road, but it causes far less slope damage than mass excavation by machine, and it generates local employment. It is the appropriate technique for rural district roads.

**HILL ROAD DRAINAGE — the most important maintenance activity in Nepal:**

> **Most hill road failures are WATER-TRIGGERED.** Drainage maintenance therefore matters more than pavement maintenance.

| Drainage element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Catch water (intercepting) drain** | Above the cut slope; **diverts hillside runoff BEFORE it reaches the road** |
| **Side drain** | Longitudinal, at the toe of the cut slope; lined in erodible ground |
| **Cross drainage** — culverts, causeways | Carries streams **across** the road |
| **Chutes and cascades** | Carry water **down** the fill slope in a controlled channel, rather than allowing it to erode |
| **Sub-surface drains** | Lower the water table; drain a seepage zone |
| **Turnouts / scuppers** | Discharge from the side drain at intervals |
| **Camber and superelevation** | Shed water from the carriageway |

**The catch water drain is the key element and the most neglected.** Placed above the cut slope, it **intercepts the hillside runoff before it can reach the road at all** — so the cut face is not eroded, the formation is not saturated, and the drainage system below is not overwhelmed. A road without one receives the runoff of the whole slope above it.

**Why drainage maintenance dominates:**

| Failure | Water's role |
|---|---|
| **Landslide above the road** | Infiltration raises pore pressure, reduces effective stress and strength |
| **Slip of the fill below the road** | Saturation and seepage; concentrated discharge over the edge |
| **Erosion of the cut face** | Runoff not intercepted |
| **Pavement failure** | Water in the layers softens the subgrade and strips the binder |
| **Culvert failure** | Blocked by debris, then overtopped, washing out the formation |

**A blocked side drain or culvert converts a designed drainage system into a hazard**, because the water then finds its own path — usually over the fill edge or into the formation. Clearing drains and culverts **before the monsoon** is therefore the single most valuable maintenance activity on a Nepali hill road, and it is cheap and labour-intensive, which suits the setting.

**Slope protection and stabilisation:**

| Measure | Character |
|---|---|
| **Bio-engineering** | Grasses, shrubs and bamboo; **roots reinforce, foliage intercepts rain, transpiration dries the soil** |
| **Gabion walls and revetments** | **Flexible and permeable** — tolerates settlement, no pore pressure build-up |
| **Dry stone masonry** | Traditional, permeable |
| **Breast walls** | Support the cut slope |
| **Toe walls** | Support the fill |
| **Rock bolting, netting, catch fences** | Rockfall protection |
| **Benching and slope flattening** | Reduces the driving force |
| **Drainage** — surface and sub-horizontal | Addresses the trigger |

**Bio-engineering is the technique most suited to Nepal's conditions**, promoted by the Department of Roads:

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| Uses **local plant species and local labour** | Cheap, and the skills exist locally |
| **Strengthens with time** as roots develop | Unlike a structure, which only deteriorates |
| Addresses **both water and reinforcement** together | Interception, transpiration and root reinforcement |
| Low cost, low technology | Maintainable by the community |

Its limitations are equally real: it takes **one or two growing seasons to become effective**, so it cannot provide immediate protection; it reinforces only the **shallow** zone that roots reach, not deep-seated instability; and it needs **protection from grazing** while establishing.

**So the standard practice is a COMBINATION** — a **structural toe** (gabion or masonry) where the water or the current attacks, with **bio-engineering on the slope above**. Each does what the other cannot.

**Landslide clearance and repair:**

| Stage | Action |
|---|---|
| **Immediate** | Clear the debris; restore a single-lane passage; warn traffic |
| **Assess** | Is the slide **active or dormant**? What triggered it? |
| **Stabilise** | **DRAINAGE first**; then toe support, slope flattening, retaining structure |
| **Restore** | Reconstruct the formation and pavement |
| **Prevent recurrence** | Catch water drain above; bio-engineering; monitor |

**Clearing the debris without addressing the cause guarantees recurrence**, and it is what most emergency maintenance amounts to. The cause is almost always **water**, and the first stabilisation measure is almost always **drainage** — which is cheap, effective on the whole mass, and addresses the trigger rather than the symptom.

**Road maintenance management in Nepal:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Road Board Nepal** | Provides dedicated funding for maintenance from a **fuel levy and road user charges** |
| **Department of Roads** | Strategic road network |
| **Local governments** | District and rural roads |
| **Length worker (mukhiya) system** | A worker responsible for a length of road, doing routine drainage and minor repair — **appropriate, cheap, and effective for hill roads** |
| Performance-based contracts | Increasingly used for routine maintenance |

**The length worker system is worth noting as an appropriate institutional design**: routine hill road maintenance consists chiefly of **clearing drains, cutting vegetation, patching small failures and reporting problems** — all labour-intensive, all needing local presence rather than plant, and all far cheaper done continuously than in campaigns. Assigning a resident worker to a few kilometres achieves that, and the same reasoning underlies the community-based maintenance groups used on rural roads.

formulas.label: The three bituminous coats
formulas.expression: PRIME on a GRANULAR base (7–10 kg/10 m²) ; TACK between BITUMINOUS layers (2–3 kg/10 m²) ; SEAL on the FINISHED surface
formulas.note: The distinguishing question is what lies BELOW. A tack coat cannot substitute for a prime coat — it does not penetrate.

formulas.label: Bituminous laying temperatures
formulas.expression: mixing 150–165 °C ; laying ≥ 130 °C ; rolling starts ≥ 100–110 °C and completes by ≈ 80 °C
formulas.note: Compaction must finish while hot; an under-compacted layer has high air voids and ravels early.

formulas.label: Compaction requirements
formulas.expression: embankment ≥ 95% modified Proctor ; subgrade ≥ 97% (100% top 500 mm major road) ; sub-base and base 98–100%
formulas.note: Compact at or near OMC — too dry and the density is unreachable, too wet and the soil pumps.

formulas.label: Roller selection
formulas.expression: SHEEP FOOT for COHESIVE soils (kneading) ; VIBRATORY for GRANULAR (rearranges particles) ; PNEUMATIC for bituminous
formulas.note: A vibratory roller on wet clay bounces; a sheep foot on sand walks out of it.

formulas.label: Binder content diagnosis
formulas.expression: RUTTING and BLEEDING → too MUCH binder.   RAVELLING and CRACKING → too LITTLE binder.
formulas.note: Exactly the balance the Marshall design at 4% air voids exists to strike.

formulas.label: Crack type diagnosis
formulas.expression: ALLIGATOR cracking = STRUCTURAL fatigue (needs an overlay). TRANSVERSE/BLOCK = material, thermal or ageing (a surface treatment may suffice).
formulas.note: Distinguishing them decides between a structural overlay and a surface treatment — a large cost difference.

formulas.label: Side slopes
formulas.expression: ordinary soil: 1:1 to 1.5:1 in CUTTING, 1.5:1 to 2:1 in FILLING
formulas.note: Filling always takes flatter slopes, being remoulded and less consolidated.

formulas.label: Maintenance economics
formulas.expression: Work deferred does not wait — it MULTIPLIES. A sealed crack prevents a pothole prevents a failed section.
formulas.note: Crack sealing gives the highest return of any maintenance activity, because water is what destroys pavements.
